lines.text: High mountains, a desert coast and the edge of the Amazon. This is the story of Peru, from its first cities and the Incas to the republic of today.
Millions of years ago, high in the Andes, Lake Titicaca took shape, one of the highest lakes in the world that boats can sail.
Some ten thousand years ago, people in these mountains began farming the potato, a gift Peru would one day give the whole world.
About five thousand years ago Caral rose near the coast, one of the oldest cities in all the Americas.
Later, the Chavin people built a great temple in the highlands, and their culture spread across the Andes.
In the southern desert, the Nazca scratched giant animals and lines into the ground, best seen from the air. Why, we still do not know.
On the north coast the Moche made lifelike portrait pots, and buried the Lord of Sipan in a tomb full of gold.
Around 850 work began on Chan Chan, which would become the largest city of mud brick in the Americas.
Up in the Andes, Cusco was founded, the city that would become the heart of the Incas.
Meanwhile the Chimu kingdom ruled the north coast from Chan Chan, until the Incas conquered it.
Then came Pachacuti, who turned a small kingdom around Cusco into an empire, and rebuilt his capital in stone.
The Inca Empire became the largest in the Americas, stretching along the Andes from Ecuador to Chile, its records kept on knotted cords.
Above Cusco they built Sacsayhuaman, with giant stones fitted so tightly that no mortar was needed.
High on a ridge in the clouds, the Inca rulers built Machu Picchu, with its terraces, temples and stone houses.
Roads, stairways and rope bridges joined it all, and relay runners carried messages across tens of thousands of kilometres.
In 1532 Francisco Pizarro and a small Spanish force captured the emperor Atahualpa. Helped by disease and civil war, they took the empire.
In 1535 Pizarro founded Lima near the Pacific, and it became the capital of Spain's South America.
In 1780 Tupac Amaru the second led a great Indigenous revolt against Spanish rule, which was crushed.
Meanwhile on the coast, raw fish cured in lime juice was becoming the dish Peru calls its own, ceviche.
In 1821 the war for independence began, and it was won at Ayacucho in 1824.
Peru declared itself free in 1821, a new republic on the old Inca lands.
In 1911 the American explorer Hiram Bingham brought Machu Picchu to the world's attention, and it became Peru's great symbol.
In 1936 Mario Vargas Llosa was born in Arequipa. His novels made him a star of Latin American writing, and won him the Nobel Prize.
Two years later came Alberto Fujimori, the president who would crush the Shining Path, rule harshly, and end up in prison.
From 1969 the Maoist Shining Path grew, and its war on the state cost tens of thousands of lives.
In 1996 rebels seized the Japanese ambassador's residence in Lima and held seventy-two hostages for four months.
And in December 2022, President Castillo tried to dissolve Congress, and was arrested the same day.
From Caral to Lima, Peru has carried five thousand years of history down from the mountains.
